papers.title: [Editorial] The unmet needs of people living with severe asthma
papers.summary: More than 260 million people worldwide live with asthma, and more than 400 000 die of the disease each year. 5–10% of people with asthma live with severe asthma, but it has an outsized effect—frequent disease exacerbations, poor lung function, and a widespread dependence on corticosteroids. Despite serious symptoms, asthma is often underdiagnosed and mismanaged, which—in the worst-case scenarios—can be fatal.

papers.title: [Comment] Stopping β-blockers long after myocardial infarction
papers.summary: Few areas of cardiovascular pharmacotherapy have changed as much as β-blocker use after myocardial infarction. For decades, β-blockers were prescribed routinely and often indefinitely after myocardial infarction, a practice based on trials from the early 1980s showing reductions in mortality and recurrent events.1 However, those trials preceded routine reperfusion, invasive management, statins, and dual antiplatelet therapy; therefore, their relevance to contemporary post-myocardial infarction patients is uncertain.

papers.title: [Comment] Early-life primary prevention of childhood asthma
papers.summary: Asthma-related symptoms, such as wheezing, are highly prevalent among preschool children. Asthma is a complex disease and originates from genetic susceptibility combined with different environmental exposures. Early life is a specific critical period for development of later-life asthma.1 Population studies have identified various fetal and early-childhood risk factors for asthma, including early-life respiratory tract infections.1 Early-life respiratory tract infections have not only short-term consequences, but seem also to affect the development of both the respiratory and immune systems, and subsequently predispose individuals to chronic respiratory diseases in later life.

papers.title: [Comment] Perioperative immunotherapy goes global in gastro-oesophageal cancer
papers.summary: Gastric and gastro-oesophageal junction cancers are among the most common causes of cancer-related deaths.1 In patients with operable tumours, several phase 3 trials established the value of perioperative chemotherapy.2–4 In parallel, phase 3 studies in advanced disease confirmed a survival advantage for anti-PD-1 and anti-PD-L1 immune checkpoint inhibitors in combination with platinum doublet chemotherapy, particularly in PD-L1 expressing tumours.5 Thus, examination of whether immune checkpoint inhibitors could improve outcomes in patients who are non-metastatic was warranted.

papers.title: [Comment] Closing the preparedness gap: moving beyond emergency response to sustain the medical countermeasure ecosystem
papers.summary: Infectious disease outbreaks expose weaknesses that are overlooked between crises. The ongoing Ebola virus disease outbreak caused by Bundibugyo virus (Orthoebolavirus bundibugyoense; BDBV) in the Democratic Republic of the Congo, during which there has been cross-border transmission into Uganda, has brought together governments, regional and multilateral organisations, manufacturers, research institutions, and financing partners. These actors are accelerating the development, evaluation, and deployment of medical countermeasures (MCMs), including diagnostics, vaccines, therapeutics, and personal protective equipment (PPE).

papers.title: [Comment] Offline: The emptiness of the quantified self
papers.summary: Byung-Chul Han's short book, Psychopolitics: Neoliberalism and New Technologies of Power (2025, first published in German in 2014), opens with a line that should make us all pause: “Freedom will prove to have been merely an interlude.” End-of arguments have not fared well in recent years. The end of history? We can only wish. But Han's case deserves a hearing because his critique attacks some of health science's most cherished principles. He claims that the era of ever-larger quantities of data is reducing human freedoms.

papers.title: [World Report] Creating the building blocks of life
papers.summary: From constructing cell-like systems to creating genomes from scratch, synthetic biology is having a moment. What will it mean for health? Talha Burki reports.

papers.title: [World Report] ALIMA: the NGO doing things differently
papers.summary: Founded only in 2009 but central to the Ebola response in DR Congo, ALIMA brings local leadership to humanitarian action. Andrei Popoviciu reports.

papers.title: [Perspectives] Waleska Teixeira Caiaffa: shaping healthier cities
papers.summary: In 1974, as the Brazilian student resistance movement strengthened against repression by the country's authoritarian government, Waleska Teixeira Caiaffa became a medical student at the Federal University of Minas Gerais in Brazil. The university was located in Belo Horizonte, Brazil's first planned modern city. Caiaffa witnessed “many student protests during which the military would come in and arrest students”, alongside the city's rapid but inequitable urban expansion. Although “the city was designed as a ‘healthy city’”, she explains, Black informal workers who had either been forcibly displaced from the city centre or migrated from rural areas settled in unplanned, precarious “favela” settlements, expanding racial segregation.

papers.title: [Perspectives] The battle for better mental health systems needs us all
papers.summary: When I was in my late 20s I stood on a bridge for a very long time. I was there, for many reasons. Fatigue being the greatest among them. This tiredness was not only caused by lack of sleep but also from exhaustion linked to 2 years spent as a Black woman in the majority white space of an elite UK academic institution. It was during my doctorate and I was seeking to elevate women's voices. I was exhausted by having to justify my methodological choices and conceptual frameworks to allow the complexity of these women's lives and their mental health needs to be seen.

papers.title: [Perspectives] Why medicine needs philosophy of medicine
papers.summary: The starting point for medicine is accurate knowledge of the body. These words belong to the renowned 2nd-century physician Galen. However, as revealed by the title of their text, The Best Physician is Also a Philosopher, Galen argued that a true follower of Hippocrates also needs philosophy. For Galen, what distinguished a druggist from a physician is that the latter is practised in logic, ethics, and natural philosophy (the study of the natural world). Galen himself was both physician and philosopher.

papers.title: [Obituary] Vadim Pokrovsky
papers.summary: Epidemiologist and leading HIV specialist in Russia. Born on Jan 17, 1955, in Moscow, Russia, he died on May 20, 2026, in Moscow, aged 71 years.

papers.title: [Correspondence] A call to humanity in the wake of Nepal's massive Himalayan flash flood
papers.summary: On Aug 26, 2026, glacial lake outburst floods affecting Rasuwa, Nuwakot, and Dhading districts in Nepal swept away entire communities, killing 1204 people (as established by recovery of deceased bodies and body parts), with around 4216 people reported missing (as of Sept 2, 2026).1 Global media reported this catastrophic disaster as a Himalayan tsunami.2 Nestled in the Himalayas, Nepal faces an ongoing climate threat and is further vulnerable due to settlements along riverbanks. There are thousands of glacial lakes storing meltwater, and their number is increasing as global temperatures rise, making them akin to ticking time bombs.

papers.title: [Correspondence] Making rehabilitation indicators disability-inclusive
papers.summary: Global efforts to strengthen rehabilitation systems are urgently needed. The WHO Rehabilitation 2030 initiative and its work to develop standardised rehabilitation indicators1 are therefore important steps towards improving rehabilitation services and advancing the aims of the UN Convention on the Rights of Persons with Disabilities. However, Wouter de Groote and colleagues’2 expectation that these indicators can ensure “a measurable path to independence and participation” risks overlooking structural and social inequalities in access to rehabilitation.

papers.title: [Correspondence] The Italian model of screening for CKD
papers.summary: Tonelli and colleagues should be commended for their recently published Health Policy.1 This advocacy paper will indeed profoundly change the vision of nephrology practice on chronic kidney disease (CKD). The paper itemises the major steps towards a major paradigm shift, that is, the transition from replacing kidney function by means of dialysis and transplantation to preserving kidney function through conservative kidney management, which reflects the original mission of the specialty.

papers.title: [Correspondence] Patient organisations are key implementation partners
papers.summary: As President of the Mario Robles Ossio Foundation, a Mexican patient organisation, I strongly support the focus on implementation in the Health Policy by Tonelli and colleagues.1 Mexico has one of the highest burdens of kidney disease worldwide. In March, 2025, chronic kidney disease was included within the National Medical Care Protocols.2 However, as the paper highlights, the real challenge begins after policy adoption: translating those commitments into actions that reach people in their daily lives.

papers.title: [Correspondence] Unmasking inequity: emergency presentations in ovarian cancer care
papers.summary: We highly commend Isabelle Ray-Coquard and colleagues for their Comment announcing the Lancet Commission on Ovarian Cancer,1 emphasising equity-driven reform. However, we believe they overlook a crucial barrier to improving population-level survival: emergency presentations.

papers.title: [Correspondence] Unmasking inequity: emergency presentations in ovarian cancer care – Authors’ reply
papers.summary: We thank Rui Wu and colleagues for their thoughtful commentary on the outlined objectives for the Lancet Commission on Ovarian Cancer.1 The authors have provided intriguing data regarding the percentage of women who are first diagnosed in emergency room settings (up to 50% in some jurisdictions) and the associated prognostic implications of this presentation. Wu and colleagues raise important findings: these patients are far more likely to be older, frailer, and to have inequities in access to stable health care (for a variety of complex reasons that vary by country) and thus might be excluded from optimised diagnostic pathways (inclusive of genetics and molecular profiling), surgical intervention, access to novel therapeutics, and optimised survivorship plans.

papers.title: [Correspondence] Physical activity and exercise training in patients with HFrEF
papers.summary: We read with great interest the Seminar by Antonio Cannata and colleagues1 on novel diagnosis and management approaches to heart failure with reduced ejection fraction (HFrEF). We were surprised by the omission of recent guideline-recommended regular physical activity counselling and supervised exercise training;2,3 therefore, we highlight here its benefits combined with pharmacotherapy.

papers.title: [Correspondence] Physical activity and exercise training in patients with HFrEF – Authors’ reply
papers.summary: We thank Tim Kambič and colleagues for their Correspondence regarding the importance of exercise and physical activity for patients with heart failure with reduced ejection fraction (HFrEF).

papers.title: [Correspondence] Platinum-resistant ovarian cancers: lessons from KEYNOTE-B96
papers.summary: We congratulate Nicoletta Colombo and colleagues for the practice changing results of the ENGOT-ov65/KEYNOTE-B96 trial in platinum-resistant ovarian cancer.1 Their study reports clinically significant improvement in progression-free survival and clinically meaningful improvement in overall survival with pembrolizumab plus weekly paclitaxel, with or without bevacizumab, in patients who had received no more than two previous lines of systemic therapies (for platinum-resistant ovarian cancer).1 These findings are notable in a setting of historically poor prognosis.

papers.title: [Correspondence] Platinum-resistant ovarian cancers: lessons from KEYNOTE-B96 – Authors’ reply
papers.summary: We thank Stanislas Quesada and colleagues for their thoughtful comments and for recognising the clinically meaningful benefit of pembrolizumab plus weekly paclitaxel, with or without bevacizumab, in platinum-resistant ovarian cancer.1 Because ENGOT-ov65/KEYNOTE-B96 was not designed to support unplanned subgroup analyses, we have limited our response to prespecified analyses and results that can be interpreted within the trial design.

papers.title: [Department of Error] Department of Error
papers.summary: Hatter L, Holliday M, Oldfield K, et al. papers.title: [Articles] Discontinuation of β-blockers in stable patients with previous myocardial infarction, preserved left ventricular ejection fraction, and no heart failure: a pooled analysis of individual patient data
papers.summary: In stable patients with previous myocardial infarction, left ventricular ejection fraction ≥40%, no heart failure, and no other indication for β-blocker therapy, discontinuation met the non-inferiority criteria for the primary and key secondary endpoints. Interpretation of the primary endpoint is limited by its hospitalisation-heavy and trial-dependent composition.

papers.title: [Articles] Use of the bacterial lysate OM-85 for the primary prevention of wheezing lower respiratory illness in preschool children: a randomised, placebo-controlled trial
papers.summary: Oral administration of OM-85 in early life did not decrease the incidence of wheezing lower respiratory tract illness in this high-risk population. Bacterial lysates are not efficacious for the primary prevention of asthma-like symptoms during the preschool years.

papers.title: [Articles] Perioperative durvalumab plus fluorouracil, leucovorin, oxaliplatin, and docetaxel for resectable gastric and gastro-oesophageal junction adenocarcinoma (MATTERHORN): final results of overall survival and event-free survival by pathological response in a global, randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled, multicentre, phase 3 trial
papers.summary: Perioperative durvalumab plus FLOT improved overall survival versus placebo plus FLOT and is a new standard treatment option for patients with resectable gastric or gastro-oesophageal junction adenocarcinoma.

papers.title: [Review] Wildfire smoke and health: current evidence, mechanisms, and future challenges
papers.summary: In the era of climate change, numerous regions worldwide are facing a surge in both the frequency and unprecedented scale of wildfires. Exposure to wildfire smoke poses substantial risks to health, especially for vulnerable populations. Although previous studies have shed light on health effects of wildfire smoke, crucial research gaps persist, including long-term health effects, interactions with pre-existing health conditions, and health disparities. Closing these gaps is vital to enhancing the ability to safeguard public health during wildfire events and to formulate effective strategies for prevention, mitigation, and response.

papers.title: [Editorial] Oral carbapenem—a double-edged sword?
papers.summary: In June 2026, the US Food and Drug Administration (FDA) approved the first oral carbapenem, tebipenem, for the treatment of complicated urinary tract infections (UTIs). While this approval paves the way for more convenient treatment without the need for hospitalisation, it also raises questions around stewardship and rates of carbapenem resistance.

papers.title: [Newsdesk] Research in brief
papers.summary: Although observational studies suggest that the four-component meningococcal serogroup B vaccine (4CMenB) might lower the risk of gonorrhoea, the randomised GoGoVax trial in Australia found that 4CMenB vaccination did not result in fewer Neisseria gonorrhoeae infections compared with placebo. The trial analysis included 587 adult men who have sex with men (MSM) who had a diagnosis of N gonorrhoeae infection or syphilis within the previous 18 months, received two doses of either the vaccine or placebo 3 months apart, and attended at least two follow-up visits.

papers.title: [Obituary] Clarence James Peters
papers.summary: World-renowned virologist died on July 4, 2026, aged 85 years.

papers.title: [Profile] Aalisha Sahukhan—strengthening public health responses
papers.summary: Aalisha Sahukhan was eight when she decided she would become a doctor. “Exactly the age to be making important life decisions”, this proud Fijian tells The Lancet Infectious Diseases, a decision shaped by her beloved grandmother's illness and passing, and wanting to be useful while steering clear of spotlight. Her career, leading the Fiji Centre for Disease Control (Fiji CDC), would ultimately thrust her into the spotlight, first as chair of taskforces leading responses to national epidemics of meningitis (2018) and measles (2019), and ultimately as technical lead and a national spokesperson for Fiji's response to COVID-19.

papers.title: [Clinical Picture] Tularaemia after deer exposure in a vehicular collision
papers.summary: A 39-year-old man sustained facial lacerations from the body of a roe deer (Capreolus capreolus) and shattered glass after the animal, first struck by an oncoming vehicle, broke through his windshield. Animal blood, bodily fluids from eviscerated organs (eg, intestines), and soil contaminated his wounds (figure A). 8 days later, subjective fever, a left periorbital lesion, and ipsilateral cervical swelling developed. On day 12, sonography found cervical lymphadenitis without abscess formation. Despite amoxicillin treatment (1 g three times a day for a week), the swelling progressed (figure B).

papers.title: Chloroplasts balance energy production and stress resilience via a cold-induced signaling pathway
papers.summary: Cold-stress signals are transmitted to chloroplasts and subsequently trigger cold responses through an RAF-like bi-kinase module where cytoplasmic RAF3 and plasma membrane RAF6 translocate to chloroplasts, where they inhibit photosynthetic activity but activate nuclear cold-responsive gene expression.

papers.title: mRNA-encoding CD19-targeting T cell engager for refractory immune thrombocytopenia
papers.summary: An mRNA-lipid nanoparticle-encoded CD19×CD3 T cell engager depletes B cells with attenuated cytokine release in preclinical models. In three patients with treatment-refractory immune thrombocytopenia, treatment with this T cell engager achieved sustained platelet recovery over 6 months, suggesting that mRNA-encoded T cell engagers represent a promising therapeutic approach for resetting autoreactive immunity in B cell-driven autoimmune disease.

papers.title: Oligodendrocytes in central nervous system health and disease
papers.summary: Oligodendrocytes, predominantly known for their role in myelination, play a broader role in regulating the central nervous system, including feeding axons and reshaping neural circuits, with their malfunction in diseases ranging from multiple sclerosis to Alzheimer’s. This review covers oligodendrocyte biology and their therapeutic relevance.

papers.title: Toward autonomous science with agentic artificial intelligence
papers.summary: Biomedical artificial intelligence is advancing from tools that answer human-posed questions to agents that ask their own. Guo et al. assess this transition, including scaling logic, autonomous-laboratory trajectory, and the risks of hallucination, bias, dual use, and cognitive deskilling. This perspective argues that progress depends on responsible human-AI collaboration.

papers.title: Phosphate backbone epitranscriptomics: Discovery of natural RNA phosphorothioates and their writer machinery
papers.summary: Phosphorothioates, stereospecific modifications of the RNA phosphate backbone in anaerobic archaea, expand the epitranscriptome beyond nucleobases and ribose sugars. Installed by Esti enzymes at conserved rRNA and tRNA hotspots, these environmentally responsive marks stabilize tRNAs and support growth at high temperatures.

papers.title: 3D chromatin remodeling during domestication defines novel targets for crop improvement
papers.summary: Population-level 3D genome atlas of 34 semi-wild and 267 cultivated allotetraploid cottons reveals domestication-selected chromatin conformations that enhance cotton fiber quality and unlock cryptic breeding targets.

papers.title: Gliomas phenocopy an inborn error of metabolism to drive neuronal activity and tumor growth
papers.summary: Glioma-derived guanidinoacetate depolarizes neighboring neurons through γ-aminobutyric acid (GABA) A receptors, and depleting this metabolite reduces both neuronal activity and glioma growth.

papers.title: Single-cell-resolved genome atlas of prokaryoplankton inhabiting the ocean’s interior
papers.summary: GORG-Dark presents genomes of 9,698 individual bacterial and archaeal cells from the ocean’s sunless interior. The atlas resolves depth stratification to abyssal waters, uncovers particle-attached Pelagibacterales, maps chemolithoautotrophy and biosynthetic gene clusters, and identifies a rhodopsin clade specific to the dark ocean.

papers.title: Programmed ribosomal frameshifting triggers translational stress to promote viral replication
papers.summary: Viruses such as SARS-CoV-2 can use programmed ribosomal frameshifting to turn off host translation and promote viral replication, expanding the known uses of programmed ribosomal frameshifting by viruses.

papers.title: Norway spruce spatiotemporal programs of conifer reproductive development
papers.summary: Spatiotemporal transcriptomics across conifer reproductive and vegetative shoots reveals candidate developmental regulators and evolutionarily conserved tissue patterning genes in seed plants.

papers.title: Copper ion-induced MYH9 polymerization executes cuproptosis
papers.summary: Copper binding drives MYH9 polymerization, triggering cytoskeletal collapse and cuproptosis. HThPA releases intracellular copper through glutathione depletion, exposing a therapeutic vulnerability in drug-resistant tumors.

papers.title: Metax enables accurate cross-domain taxonomic profiling of metagenomes
papers.summary: Metax is a cross-domain metagenomic profiler that uses genome-wide coverage evidence to improve species-level microbial profiling and distinguish supported taxa from artifacts. Across diverse datasets, Metax enables robust taxonomic profiling, pathogen detection, contamination assessment, and discovery of disease-associated bacterial and viral signatures.

papers.title: Mitochondrial ATP promotes T cell differentiation through chromatin accessibility
papers.summary: Cell-mediated immunity requires cytotoxic CD8+ T cells that adopt and maintain an effector phenotype. Here, D-α-hydroxybutyrate (DAHB) is shown to act as a metabolic adjuvant, driving the conversion of proliferating CD8+ T cells into cytotoxic effector cells by linking mitochondrial ATP production to chromatin remodeling and gene expression.

papers.title: Glycocalyx-edited mesenchymal stem/stromal cell therapy in advanced osteoporosis
papers.summary: Mesenchymal stem/stromal cell (MSC)-based therapy holds promise for reversal of bone loss in osteoporosis. This phase 1 study establishes the safety and feasibility of intravenous administration of glycocalyx-engineered human MSCs and provides evidence that MSCs derived from the bone marrow of older individuals with osteoporosis retain clinically meaningful osteoregenerative capacity.

papers.title: Architecture of the serotonergic projectome in the mouse brain
papers.summary: Serotonin neurons innervate nearly the entire mammalian brain, yet how their projections are organized has remained unclear. Systematic whole-brain serotonergic axon collateralization mapping reveals five projectomic groups that preferentially target functionally related regions, with each projectomic group connecting to specific spatial transcriptomic and behavioral profiles.

papers.title: Caloric restriction modulates genome-wide somatic mutation in mice
papers.summary: Mutations accumulate in cells with age, while caloric restriction extends lifespan across diverse animals. Grońska-Pęski et al. study the effect of caloric restriction on mutations genome-wide in mice, finding reduced mutation burdens across several tissues and cell types, thereby establishing that diet can alter mutation accumulation genome-wide during aging.

papers.title: Structural basis of a SWI/SNF-associated transcription pre-initiation complex
papers.summary: Cryo-EM and genetic analyses reveal that the SWI/SNF chromatin remodeler is an integral component of the transcription pre-initiation complex. The structures demonstrate how SWI/SNF facilitates transcription initiation through stabilization of PIC organization and concerted remodeling of the +1 nucleosome.

papers.title: Identification of the tendon/ligament stem cell in mice and humans
papers.summary: The tendon/ligament stem cell is identified, and dysregulation of differentiation in this cell is shown as a mechanism contributing to lumbar spinal stenosis.

papers.title: Tabula Sapiens 2.0: A comprehensive transcriptomic atlas of human cell types
papers.summary: An expanded atlas of human cells maps the expression of nearly all human transcription factors across 701 cell-type/tissue combinations and uncovers the heterogeneous nature of senescence across tissues and cell types.

papers.title: Oxygen-responsive bacterial glycosphingolipid links symbiont fitness and immune development in neonatal host
papers.summary: How do maternal gut bacteria seed the rapidly developing neonatal gut? Heo et al. show that Bacteroides fragilis produces a distinct membrane lipid that enables this strict anaerobe to tolerate a microaerobic environment. This finding highlights divergent evolutionary strategies among related species, most of which rely on lipids conferring broader fitness.

papers.title: Ratiometric transcriptional activation by protein degradation
papers.summary: By tethering a protein of interest to anti-CRISPR, protein degradation is transformed into amplified and programmable transcriptional outputs via Cas-based transcription factors, with sensitivity to protein loss tuned by the anti-CRISPR-Cas ratio. These synthetic circuits can be multiplexed to enable high-throughput discovery of protein-degrading and -destabilizing molecules.

papers.title: De novo pan-rhodamine binders for fluorescence microscopy from mammalian cells to extremophiles
papers.summary: We developed an AI-based and principled computational strategy for de novo design of Rhobins, compact pan-rhodamine binders with high brightness, reversible binding, and extreme stability. It enables superior live-/fixed-cell, super-resolution, and single-molecule imaging with properties surpassing existing tags. It also supports extremophile imaging at 75°C, inaccessible with current tools.

papers.title: Cross-species single-cell atlas of the striatum defines cell-type and subregion disease vulnerabilities
papers.summary: Single-nucleus RNA sequencing and spatial validation across human and mouse striatum define principles of neuronal specialization across cell types, subregions, and species. These findings lay the foundation for understanding cell- and subregion-resolved contributions to brain function and disease, including addiction risk, antipsychotic responses, Huntington’s disease vulnerabilities, and pharmacologically relevant species differences.

papers.title: Live-cell transcriptomics with engineered virus-like particles
papers.summary: Najia, Le, Borrajo et al. establish “cellular self-reporting,” a technology to export molecular analytes from cells in virus-like particles. The authors demonstrate how mRNA export enables longitudinal transcriptome-wide profiling of living cells by sampling cell media. This platform transcends the destructive nature of conventional transcriptomic analysis methods and reveals gene expression dynamics in complex biological systems in situ.

papers.title: Endogenous opioid dynamics in the dorsal striatum sculpt neural activity to promote goal-directed action
papers.summary: Cell-type-specific, time-locked release of the opioid neuropeptide dynorphin in the dorsomedial striatum is both necessary and sufficient for goal-directed behavior. Inputs from the basolateral amygdala trigger dynorphin release that engages retrograde Gi-coupled presynaptic inhibition via the kappa opioid receptor, revealing a rapid neuropeptide mechanism for shaping behavior.

papers.title: Genome-scale perturb-seq in primary human CD4+ T cells maps context-specific regulators of T cell programs and human immune traits
papers.summary: A dynamic atlas of gene regulation was generated by perturbing every expressed gene across 22 million primary human CD4+ T cells under resting conditions and following re-stimulation. The resulting map reveals context-specific regulators of immune programs and links regulatory pathways to naturally occurring T cell states and autoimmune disease risk.

papers.title: Human nuclear ribomes reveal DNA-embedded ribonucleotides as epigenetic modulators of transcription-associated DNA supercoiling
papers.summary: Human nuclear ribomes reveal that DNA-embedded ribonucleotides accumulate at promoter-associated regulatory elements and scale with transcriptional activity. RNase H2 and Top1 process these ribonucleotides to modulate DNA supercoiling, uncovering a previously unrecognized epigenetic mechanism underlying transcription.

papers.title: Integrative spatial profiling of 3D genome organization and gene expression in tissue
papers.summary: Spatial Hi-C-RNA simultaneously maps genome architecture and gene expression from the same tissue, revealing how spatial genome organization shapes cellular identity, development, and tumor evolution beyond what transcriptomics alone can capture.

papers.title: DDIAS shields single-stranded DNA in mitosis and promotes vertebrate brain development
papers.summary: DDIAS is identified as a factor that protects single-stranded DNA during mitosis to maintain chromosome stability, and inactivating mutations in DDIAS are identified in a human neurodevelopmental disorder.

papers.title: Dietary pectin remodels commensal bacterial surfaces to promote IgA-mediated protection from intestinal inflammation
papers.summary: Tang et al. reveal that dietary pectin drives Bacteroides uniformis surface remodeling to enrich the surface glycosphingolipid HexCer. Neutrophils sense this signal via CLEC4E to promote IgA production, which helps this bacterium colonize the gut lining and protects against colitis, uncovering a diet-microbe pathway that promotes a mutually beneficial relationship.

papers.title: The rice circadian clock orchestrates the rhizosphere microbiome to synchronize nitrogen supply with plant demand

papers.title: Microbial indole-3-acetamide alleviates polycystic ovary syndrome through HIF-2α-ceramide signaling
papers.summary: Chen et al. reveal that C. aerofaciens mitigates PCOS pathology through activation of the adipose HIF-2α-ceramide signaling pathway. papers.title: Hippuric acid metabolism by Corynebacterium glucuronolyticum-like bacteria promotes calcium oxalate crystallization

papers.title: A microbial chromatin remodeler drives gastric cancer progression and immune evasion by reprogramming the host epigenome

papers.title: Bacteroides acidifaciens enriched by KRAS mutation promotes colorectal tumorigenesis

papers.title: Dual sensing activates antiviral reverse transcriptase for membrane targeting

papers.title: Mobile virus-derived siRNAs drive plant antiviral silencing through reiterated 3–4 cell immunization

papers.title: Bacterial effector modifies host messenger RNA to promote virulence
papers.summary: McCaffrey et al. describe the isolation of a secreted bacterial enzyme from Legionella pneumophila that mediates 8-oxo-guanine (oxo8G) modifications of host mRNAs to inhibit their expression. papers.title: Cancers modulate processing and presentation of p53 neoantigens to evade T cell detection
papers.summary: Mutations in TP53 occur early in malignant transformation and are generally present in all descendant tumor cells. Haratani et al. find a dearth of actionable neoantigens displayed in the cancer immunopeptidome and define various mechanisms whereby tumor cells prevent effective processing and presentation of p53 neoantigens.

papers.title: Twenty-year persistence of SARS-CoV-1 immune imprinting shapes antibody responses to SARS-CoV-2 infection
papers.summary: Our understanding of long-term sarbecovirus immune imprinting remains limited. Zhang et al. reveal persistent imprinting in individuals sequentially infected with SARS-CoV-1 and SARS-CoV-2 over two decades, characterized by redirected antibody targeting from the variable receptor-binding motif to conserved receptor-binding domain (RBD) core regions after breakthrough infection. papers.title: A pulmonary innate lymphoid cell-driven serotonergic neuroimmune axis orchestrates airway hyperreactivity and cough hypersensitivity
papers.summary: ILC2s engage in bidirectional neuroimmune crosstalk that shapes diverse physiological functions, yet whether ILC2-mediated serotonergic signaling affects asthma pathophysiology remains unexplored. papers.title: A distinct effector B cell population drives autoantibody production in SARS-CoV-2 infection
papers.summary: Autoantibodies (autoAbs) are linked to mortality and Long COVID, yet their cellular origins remain unclear. papers.title: T cell fate is dictated by different antigen-presenting cells in response to dietary versus gut epithelial self-antigen
papers.summary: Mechanisms governing T cell responses to food or microbes have been characterized; however, whether they also regulate gut autoimmunity is unknown. papers.title: Long-lasting extracellular matrix modifications reshape intestinal stem cell fate and promote chronic inflammation
papers.summary: Whether inflammation leaves a lasting imprint on the intestinal stem cell (ISC) niche has remained unknown. Yet very low rates of disclosure of AI use by authors have been reported. papers.summary: This study estimates the share of US-born and non–US-born US medical graduates (USMGs) and international medical graduates (IMGs) in the US internal medicine workforce, as well as the share of underserved patients cared for by these physicians.

papers.title: A Review of Endometrial Cancer
papers.summary: To the Editor A recent Review offered a comprehensive overview of endometrial cancer, highlighting the emerging significance of molecular classification in informing prognosis and treatment, which reflects the growing role of molecular classification in clinical care. Nevertheless, the practical implementation of molecular classification was inadequately explored. Access to comprehensive molecular testing is inconsistent across health care systems. Even in high-resource settings, the availability of assays such as polymerase epsilon (POLE) sequencing is variable and result interpretation lacks standardization. These challenges are more pronounced in low-resource settings, resulting in a disparity between theoretical optimal care and real-world clinical practice.

papers.title: A Review of Endometrial Cancer
papers.summary: To the Editor In a recent Review of endometrial cancer, the major hormonal risk factors associated with this malignancy were discussed. However, polyendocrine metabolic ovarian syndrome (PMOS), formerly known as polycystic ovary syndrome (PCOS), the most common endocrine disorder affecting reproductive-aged women, was not addressed. This omission is noteworthy given the substantial evidence linking PMOS to an increased risk of endometrial cancer, particularly among premenopausal women. This association primarily concerns low-grade endometrioid carcinomas, which typically arise through estrogen-dependent pathways.

The absolute excess associated with prior adenoma was therefore modest, making these data clinically important for decisions about surveillance intensity. However, 2 issues deserve attention before these findings are translated into broad deimplementation.

papers.title: Colorectal Cancer and Mortality Among Older Adults With vs Without Adenoma on Prior Colonoscopy
papers.summary: To the Editor A recent study provided valuable competing risk data for surveillance decisions in adults aged 75 years or older with prior colonoscopy. In their cohort, 10-year colorectal cancer incidence was higher among individuals with prior adenoma than among those without adenoma, but the absolute difference was small (1.1% vs 0.7%). Colorectal cancer mortality was similarly low, whereas noncolorectal cancer death was approximately 48%, and increased to 82% among those with severe frailty. The accompanying Editorial appropriately framed these findings as a challenge to reflexive surveillance in late life.

papers.title: Colorectal Cancer and Mortality Among Older Adults With vs Without Adenoma on Prior Colonoscopy
papers.summary: To the Editor With regard to colorectal cancer surveillance in older adults, a recent study presented compelling data highlighting that the risk of noncolorectal cancer death far exceeds the risk of colorectal cancer in adults aged 75 years or older, even among those with a prior adenoma. This finding is important for shared decision-making and supports the deescalation of surveillance in this population. However, we wish to raise 2 points regarding the interpretation of these results that are highly relevant to current clinical practice.

papers.title: Colorectal Cancer and Mortality Among Older Adults With vs Without Adenoma on Prior Colonoscopy—Reply

We welcome this suggestion and, in the Discussion section of our article, highlighted the importance of an ongoing trial in the US comparing fecal immunochemical testing vs colonoscopy-based surveillance for older adults with prior polypectomy.

papers.title: High-Dose Vitamin C in Burns
papers.summary: In this issue of JAMA, Stoppe and colleagues present the results of an international randomized clinical trial that provides evidence that high-dose intravenous vitamin C does not improve outcomes in patients with large burns. papers.summary: Pre-existing Orthoflavivirus immunity can shape antibody recall upon infection with a heterologous virus. The FDA has cleared Medtronic’s LigaSure RAS Maryland jaw vessel sealer-divider to be used in combination with the device maker’s Hugo robotic-assisted surgery system.

The FDA granted Aptitude its first 510(k) clearance for the next-generation Metrix COVID diagnostic that features three-times greater sensitivity with 30% faster results that its original emergency use authorized test.

After former Legend Biotech CEO Ying Huang, Ph.D., left the company suddenly in July, Legend has found its permanent CEO, poaching Novartis veteran Ingrid Zhang as the CAR-T specialist eyes its next phase of growth.
The company has voluntarily stopped enrolling new patients in the studies in response to reports of mostly mild or moderate adverse events.
Bristol Myers Squibb has axed the degrader-antibody conjugate it bought from Orum Therapeutics for $100 million, walking away from the asset after seeing phase 1 data.
Electra Therapeutics is the latest biotech to overshoot its own IPO expectations this year, with the inflammation-focused company bringing in $350 million from this morning’s Nasdaq listing.
A new biotech has sprung out of stealth with a bold vision to develop the “greatest therapeutic of all time”—a drug that can quickly sober up people who have had too much to drink.
A rare inherited germline mutation was found to increase risk for lung cancer by 25 times, while smoking only increased risk by 4 times.
Clinical trials are facing an enrollment crisis. Around 80% of trials don’t meet their enrollment timelines, and fewer than 5% of eligible adult cancer patients participate in trials.
After a failed merger that led to massive layoffs and a lawsuit, solid tumor biotech Lisata Therapeutics has found a new future through a merger with cardio specialist Marea Therapeutics.
Novo CEO Mike Doustdar—tapped to breathe new life into the Danish drugmaker last year after losing GLP-1 marketing ground to chief rival Eli Lilly—isn’t one to make changes for the sake of change.
Roche is paying Dualitas Therapeutics $36.5 million upfront to screen over 300,000 novel bispecific combinations in search of new treatments for immunology and inflammation diseases.

Novartis has extended its losing streak, stopping an amyotrophic lateral sclerosis program after flunking a phase 2 trial.
Novartis is paying Sironax $125 million to take up its option on a brain delivery platform, gaining control of technology for getting large molecules to targets in the central nervous system.

papers.summary: Small gene regulatory circuits can encode a surprising diversity of dynamical behaviors. A biophysical model of the AC-DC motif reveals over thirty distinct bifurcation structures and shows how molecular regulatory architecture and binding affinity orderings determine oscillations, hysteresis, and multifunctional responses to a single signal.

papers.summary: Takei et al. introduce LagTag, a chromatin-based recording strategy for mammalian cells. Past chromatin states are recorded by time-gated m6A writing and recovered alongside present states from the same cell population by antibody-guided tagmentation, establishing a foundation for temporally resolved chromatin profiling.

Müller et al. show that overexpressed membrane proteins partially displace the native membrane proteome, an effect that triggers growth collapse when a critical threshold is exceeded and traps bacteria in a non-growing state.

papers.title: Identifying memory gene expression from single-sample scRNA-seq data using power-law signatures

papers.title: The proteome as a whole: from a passive reflection of the transcriptome to an active cellular organizer

Using Mycoplasma gallisepticum as a minimal cell model, we analyzed large-scale datasets across multiple stress conditions to investigate whether the proteome functions as an integrated regulatory system. The proteome remained quantitatively stable under stress, yet the bacteria adapted successfully. We identified a minimal core of 17 major proteins constituting 35% of cellular protein mass. These proteins exhibit distinct physicochemical properties--higher positive charge, lower hydrophilicity, and enrichment in intrinsically disordered regions--suggesting they shape cytoplasmic organization and may drive liquid-liquid phase separation. Reassigning sense codons to an alternative amino acid identity establishes a genetic firewall that simultaneously prevents incoming and outgoing gene flow, but reported implementations compromise fitness, precluding clinical and industrial use. Here, we overcome this limitation using genome design and laboratory evolution to create a high-fitness genetically firewalled Escherichia coli commensal. papers.summary: Mixed-linkage (1,3;1,4)-{beta}-glucan (MLG) is a cell wall polysaccharide found in fungi, bacteria, and plants, yet the enzymatic machinery and structural determinants governing fungal MLG biosynthesis remain poorly understood. papers.summary: Engineered living materials (ELMs) offer a promising route to biologically manufactured materials for healthcare, construction and manufacturing. However, their rational design is limited by the lack of quantitative relationships linking design parameters to material properties. Here, we show that a tabular foundation model (TabPFN), informed by a small library of living hydrogels, accurately predicts macroscopic material properties from genetic and process parameters. Models were evaluated for predicting storage modulus (G'), fibre content, thickness, and permeability of Escherichia coli-produced living hydrogels containing CsgA-based fibres fused to genetically encoded PEG-like biopolymers. papers.title: Programmable DNA Assemblies Reconstitute Supramolecular Protein Function
papers.summary: Biological processes are often regulated through reactions involving supramolecular protein complexes organized with nanoscale precision, such as the apoptosome that activates procaspase-9 through defined stoichiometry to induce apoptosis. Here we report designer CASCAD (CARD Assembly on SCAffold DNA), a self-assembled DNA nanoplatform that spatially organizes caspase recruitment domains (CARDs), exhibiting catalytic intracellular caspase-9 activation. By functioning like a natural apoptosome, CASCAD enhances caspase-9 oligomerization and promotes valency-dependent enzymatic activation. papers.title: A methylome-guided toolkit for genetic engineering of the fast-growing cyanobacterium UTEX 3222
papers.summary: Cyanobacterium aponinum UTEX 3222 is a fast-growing marine cyanobacterium that reaches high cell densities, making it an attractive chassis strain for low-cost biomanufacturing. However, past efforts to genetically engineer UTEX 3222 have been unsuccessful. We hypothesized that the complex restriction modification systems in the UTEX 3222 genome constitute a major barrier to genetic transformation. Using a combined methylation avoidance and methylation mimicking approach, we overcame this barrier and successfully transformed UTEX 3222 by natural transformation, generating a large panel of fully segregated axenic strains. Transformation method was also established for a novel shuttle vector that replicates in UTEX 3222. A large-scale promoter screen identified promoters which exhibited strong expression at high cell density. These advances establish the foundation for developing UTEX 3222 as a scalable platform for photosynthetic biomanufacturing.

papers.title: Universal donor plasmids for biallelic degron-tagging in mammalian cells and organoids
papers.summary: Degron tags enable rapid, tuneable and reversible control of protein expression, and have become a critical tool for target validation and elucidating biological mechanisms. Tag engineering uses genome editing to generate biallelic gene fusions, though this process remains laborious and requires new donor vectors to be generated for each locus. papers.summary: Engineering microbial populations to perform complex functions requires programming not only cellular behaviour but also the functional organization through which biological activities are distributed across populations. papers.summary: Synthetic microbial consortia have the potential to bring novel architectures to biotechnological processes. papers.summary: Abstract Eukaryotic cell division is regulated by CDK activity that must reach critical CDK threshold levels to progress through cell cycle stages. papers.summary: Abstract RNA secondary structure is essential for understanding the functions of non-coding RNAs, ribosomal RNAs, and viral genomes. papers.summary: Abstract Processing, packaging, and nuclear export of messenger ribonucleoprotein particles (mRNPs) are critical for eukaryotic gene expression, with the DEAD-box ATPase DDX39B (yeast Sub2) playing a central role in mRNP processing and remodeling. papers.summary: Abstract Homologous recombination is a DNA repair process that requires binding of RAD51 to ssDNA at the break site. papers.summary: Abstract Bacteria produce the alarmone nucleotides ppGpp and pppGpp during stress to affect replication, transcription, and metabolism. ppGpp and pppGpp also attenuate translation by competitively binding translational GTPases to conserve resources during stress. papers.summary: Abstract Intronic GGGGCC repeat expansions in C9orf72 cause amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS) and frontotemporal dementia (FTD). papers.summary: Abstract The growing interest in nucleic acids as therapeutic targets has prompted the development of novel computational methods to facilitate drug discovery. In this study, we extend the Site Identification by Ligand Competitive Saturation (SILCS) methodology to characterize ligand–nucleic acid interactions using the Drude polarizable force field. We demonstrate the ability of the Drude force field to better model solute–nucleic acid interactions, resulting in improved identification of known binding sites and ligand binding favorability predictions across a diverse set of nucleic acid structures. papers.summary: Abstract The minute-scale lifetime of mRNA strongly influences bacterial gene expression, whereas a robust and programmable approach to directly control the mRNA stability and topology remains elusive. papers.summary: Abstract DNA mismatch repair (MMR) maintains genomic stability, and defects in MMR genes such as MLH1 and MSH2 predispose to cancer. papers.summary: Abstract Many bacteriophages encode anti-CRISPR (Acr) proteins that inhibit bacterial CRISPR–Cas immune systems. papers.summary: Abstract RNA synthesis by eukaryotic polymerases requires existing polynucleotides to serve as templates or primers. papers.title: Building sustainable diagnostic ecosystems for global health
papers.summary: Nature Reviews Bioengineering, Published online: 17 September 2026; doi:10.1038/s44222-026-00498-4 Global access to diagnostics is constrained not only by the availability of testing technologies but also by their dependence on costly supply chains that typically originate from a small number of capital-intensive biotechnology hubs. Here, we argue that integrating decentralized diagnostics with local manufacturing and research capacity is essential to building resilient, equitable and sustainable diagnostic ecosystems.

papers.summary: Nature Reviews Bioengineering, Published online: 17 September 2026; doi:10.1038/s44222-026-00495-7 Artificial intelligence (AI) and, in particular, machine learning (ML) are being explored in the development of nanoparticle-based drug delivery systems, from formulation design to preclinical evaluation. This Review discusses how ML can predict nanoparticle properties, identify optimal formulations, discover new excipients and forecast biological and therapeutic outcomes by integrating complex datasets.

papers.title: AI-enabled clinical trials
